## The idea

A two-minute piece cannot depend on two minutes of unique note data. Repetition
creates memory and makes departure audible. When an opening returns after a
contrasting section, the listener hears both recognition and elapsed time.

*Form* is the organisation of sections across a complete piece. Binary form uses
two large regions, ternary uses a return such as ABA, and rondo alternates a
recurring A with contrasting episodes. Sections resemble functions. A form plan
is a call sequence, and a varied return calls familiar material with changed
arguments.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 60
use_synth :prophet

sections = {
  a: [:c4, :e4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :f4, :g4, :c5],
  b: [:a3, :c4, :e4, :g4, :f4, :d4, :b3, :g3],
  c: [:f4, :a4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :b3, :c4, :e4],
  transition: [:g3, :a3, :b3, :d4, :f4, :e4, :d4, :g3]
}

define :play_section do |notes, transpose, amp|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play note(pitch) + transpose, sustain: 2.5,
      release: 0.35, amp: amp
    sleep 3
  end
end

form = [
  [:a, 0, 0.65],
  [:b, 0, 0.55],
  [:a, 12, 0.5],
  [:transition, 0, 0.6],
  [:c, 0, 0.7]
]

form.each do |name, transpose, amp|
  puts "section #{name} transpose=#{transpose}"
  play_section sections[name], transpose, amp
end
```

Each section lasts twenty-four beats, so five calls at 60 BPM produce two
minutes. A returns an octave higher and quieter. It is recognisably the same
data, yet its arguments mark the return as changed. The transition receives its
own name because it has a distinct connective job.

## Change one thing

1. Call A twice in succession before B. Literal repetition strengthens the
   opening and delays contrast; decide whether it establishes or exhausts the
   material.
2. Return A with `transpose: 0` and the original amplitude. Compare a literal
   ternary return with the varied one.
3. Change the plan to A-B-A-C-A. The recurring section turns the design toward
   rondo and gives C a different context.

## Why it works

The `sections` hash stores content once. The `form` array stores order and
realisation arguments. `play_section` interprets both. That separation prevents
copy-pasted score data and makes large-scale edits visible as changes to a short
call sequence.

A section name expresses identity. Arguments express variation. Transposition
preserves interval relationships, while amplitude changes perspective. Other
arguments could select instrumentation, articulation, or omitted phrases. Once
variation changes the notes beyond recognition, a new section name may describe
the result more honestly.

Control-flow analogies have limits. A listener experiences a return with memory
of intervening sound, while a runtime does not assign emotional weight to a
second call. The analogy remains useful for construction: define units, order
them, parameterise legitimate variation, and keep the plan separate from the
renderer.

Section boundaries need audible evidence. A new key, register, texture, cadence,
or rhythmic profile can announce B even when the code switches hashes at an
exact beat. Conversely, changing a symbol in the plan does not create contrast
if both arrays behave alike. The program prints labels for inspection, but the
sound must communicate the same divisions without the log pane.

Transitions deserve explicit data when they transform the route between sections.
The named transition here occupies as much time as A, B, or C, which may make it
feel like a fourth section. Shorten it to four notes and compare. Form labels are
analytical choices backed by proportion and function, not types enforced by the
renderer.

Large-scale repetition also changes listener memory. A returned A after twenty
seconds is immediate confirmation; after a minute it can feel recovered. The
same call has another effect because its position differs. Keep form order in a
visible array so those distances can be measured and revised.

## Take it further

Compose an A-B-A-C-A rondo lasting at least ninety seconds. A must use one source
array and return with two different argument sets. B and C must contrast through
both pitch range and rhythm. Store the form as data, include one named transition,
and use no copied section arrays. Print section names as the piece runs.
